title: Two spirits talk
hook: two mountain spirits check the Buddha's character before they go to meet him

segments.voice: Yesterday: the kindness poem, whole, and your line, as a mother her only child. Did you send the wish to a room full of strangers? Today, two spirits on a mountain, gossiping. Day five hundred eighty-six.

Before you hire someone, you call their references. Before you try a new doctor, you ask a friend: is she any good? Not her diploma. Her. Does she listen? Is she honest? The ninth poem of the Sutta Nipata is a reference check, done by two yakkhas, nature spirits of the hills. It's the fifteenth night of the month, a holy day. One spirit, Satagira, says to his friend: tonight's a special night. Let's go see the teacher Gotama. And his friend Hemavata, from the Himalaya, says: wait. First, tell me about him. Today: two spirits talk.
screen: `CALL THE REFERENCES.` → `A HOLY NIGHT ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `WAIT. TELL ME ABOUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Hemavata's questions come in a steady rhythm, and Satagira answers every one. Is his mind well disposed toward all beings? It is. Does he master his reactions to what he likes and what he doesn't? He does. Does he take what isn't given? He doesn't. Is he restrained toward living things, never careless, never neglecting meditation? He is. Does he lie? Speak harshly? Carry tales between people? Chatter about nothing? No, no, no and no. His words, Satagira says, are measured and full of sense. Is he free from craving, his mind clear, does he have the eye that sees the truth? Yes. Notice what Hemavata doesn't ask. Not: can he do miracles? Not: how famous is he? Not even: what does he teach? Every question is about character. How he treats beings. How he speaks. Whether his mind is steady. That's the test the poem sets for a teacher. And notice Satagira. He doesn't exaggerate or sell. He simply answers, honestly, one question at a time, and in doing it he speaks well of someone good. Then the two spirits go down the mountain and ask the Buddha their own questions. What does the world arise in? In six, he says: the six senses. At the end, the poem says, the spirits decide to travel from village to village and mountain to mountain, honoring the Buddha and the teaching. A good reputation, carried by a friend's honest words, became a journey.
screen: `WAIT: TELL ME ABOUT HIM FIRST` · `HOW HE TREATS BEINGS, HOW HE SPEAKS` · `CHARACTER, NOT MIRACLES` · `AN HONEST FRIEND'S GOOD WORD` · then, large: `THEY SPOKE WELL OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak well of someone good, starting in your head. Sit and settle. Choose someone you respect: a teacher, a coworker, a relative. Ask Hemavata's questions about them, quietly. Are they kind to people? Do they tell the truth? Do they avoid gossip? Let honest answers come, not flattery. Notice which answers make you glad. Then pick one true, specific good thing about them that you could say out loud to someone else today. Hold it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
yakkha. Hemavata asks about the Buddha's character, Satagira answers honestly, and a good word, well spoken, sends them down the mountain. Today's word.
Your line: they spoke well of him. Say your one true good thing about that person to someone else today, when they're not in the room. Day five hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist texts encourage people to examine a teacher's conduct and speech over time before placing trust in them, and on uposatha days, the holy days of the lunar month, lay Buddhists may visit a temple, keep extra precepts and hear teaching.

fork.setup: you're Hemavata. your friend wants you to meet a famous teacher tonight. what do you ask first?
options: how many followers does he have?
is his mind well disposed toward all beings?
fork.reveal: Hemavata's questions are all about character: kindness to beings, honest speech, a steady mind.

original.note: Pali yakkha (Sanskrit yaksha): a nature spirit of trees, hills or wild places, sometimes kind, sometimes fierce.

trapdoor: what you thought: two spirits talking is a fairy tale.
what it means: it's a reference check: one friend asks about a teacher's character, the other answers honestly.
what a scholar hears: the Hemavata Sutta's questions echo the list of the Buddha's virtues in the Long Discourses, and yakkhas appear across early texts as local spirits who become followers.

notes: Sn 1.9 paraphrased. Confirm the names Satagira and Hemavata, the setting on the fifteenth-day uposatha, and the sequence of questions (mind toward beings; mastery of likes and dislikes; not taking the not-given; restraint, heedfulness, jhana; the four kinds of wrong speech; freedom from craving, the eye of dhamma).
Confirm the answer 'in six the world arose' and the closing verse about wandering village to village, mountain to mountain.
The link to the moral virtues (silas) of DN 1 and 2 is an observation; confirm or remove.
